newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: U.S., Australia vie for Pakistan wheat business.
newsitem.headline: U.S., Australia vie for Pakistan wheat business.

text.p: The United States and Australia are in a head-to-head contest to win a Pakistani tender for 270,000 tonnes of wheat for January 8-31 shipment, but a U.S. diplomat said he feared the playing field would not be level.

U.S. Agricultural Attache Maurice House said the Australians had submitted only a contingent bid at Pakistan's last tender for 225,000 tonnes of U.S. soft white wheat or Australian white milling wheat, which he said should not have been acceptable.
"That's unfair," he said. "It meant the tender was decided on a quasi-negotiated basis. If they (the Australians) are going to compete, they should compete with class."
He said the Australian Wheat Board had also offered "trade-distorting" prices significantly below market levels at its previous two tenders in Egypt and Sri Lanka.
Pakistan bought 225,000 tonnes of Australian wheat from Cargill at about $152 per tonne for December 11-31 shipment at its December 1 tender.

Australian trade commissioner Don Cairns said bids had been submitted by traders, not by the Australian Wheat Board. "If they had not been in line with the bid documents, I assume they wouldn't have been accepted," he added.
Officials at Pakistan's Ministry of Food and Agriculture could not immediately be reached for comment.
"It was a direct shootout between us and the United States," Cairns said of the last tender. "I guess we won by a small margin."
He said the forthcoming tender would be fought on similar ground. "The Americans might sharpen their pencils a bit more this time, but hopefully we can pick up another one," he said.
He said Australia's wheat crop was likely to run to 21 million tonnes this year. "We have plenty to sell," he added. "We might even be able to get back into the Iraqi market."
Cairns said he expected Pakistan to tender again in early January, this time for about 250,000 tonnes of wheat.
House said the system of freight tendering in Pakistan also worked against the United States.
"Because of its relative proximity, Australia has a freight advantage of about $4 a tonne," he said. "We can sell at $4-5 a tonne cheaper than them and so remain competitive.

"Even if the freight spread is $7 a tonne we are in with a chance because we have a better financial package. In the last tender, the spread went to $10 a tonne, which is what really killed us. There needs to be more transparency."

House said the problem lay in the last right of refusal accorded to the state-run Pakistan National Shipping Corporation (PNSC). "As long as they have last right of refusal, other people won't bid seriously for freight," he added.
